title: Unpicking Is Part of the Craft. Hours the Finished Piece Never Shows
body: A finished macrame piece shows you none of its history. The plant hanger in the shop window, the wall piece at the market stall, has no memory of the evening it was unravelled back to a ball of cord. Every maker knows the real price of a handmade thing is not the materials and not even the visible hours. It is the unpicking hours, and those hours never appear on any tag. I used to treat unpicking as failure. Real makers, I thought, do not unravel. Real makers thread through the mistake. That belief produced a shelf of pieces I quietly stopped looking at, each one carrying a compromise woven in at row six that my eyes found instantly, every time, forever. A compromise you wove in Tuesday is a compromise you look at for years. The shift was an old craft book, the kind with grainy photographs, where a weaver wrote that she budgeted a third of her thread for practice and a fifth of her hours for taking work apart. A fifth. Deliberate, planned, unashamed undo time, printed in a book like a normal cost of doing business. She did not treat unpicking as the opposite of making. She treated it as a department of making, staffed and scheduled. So I tried it as an experiment. The next plant hanger, when row four went wrong, I did not negotiate with myself. I put on a podcast, made tea, and unpicked with attention. And unpicking with attention, it turns out, is not the opposite of weaving. It is weaving in reverse, and reverse is where you finally see what forward hid. I could see exactly which pull had tightened the wrong cord, which cord had been cut a hand too short, how my tension had drifted after the tea went cold. The mistake replayed under my fingers like a film at half speed. No finished piece ever taught me that much per hour. There is a technique to it too, which nobody teaches. Unpick slowly enough to save the cord's twist. Fast unpicking kinks the rope and the kink never fully leaves, so the salvaged cord carries a scar that will show in the next piece. Unpick toward the mistake, not away from it. Secure the loose end immediately, a small knot, or the whole structure walks itself backwards while you go fetch the tea. And count as you go. Unpicking is arithmetic under emotional load, and the count is the only thing that keeps you from undoing one row too many. The economics work out too, which surprised me. A two-hour unpick that saves four hours of building on a wrong foundation is not a loss. It is the cheapest two hours in the studio. The pieces that I refused to unpick did not save the two hours. They cost the whole piece, and worse, they cost the next piece, because the wrong habit rode on into it, now confident, now trained-in. The plant hangers that came after the experimental one are visibly different. There is a straightness in them that is not skill exactly. It is the absence of woven-in compromises. Every knot in them is one I chose, not one I excused. The ball of unpicked cord sits in my basket like a receipt. Half a hanger's worth of tuition, paid in the least glamorous hours of the craft. The window piece never shows it. The hands remember. The hands remember everything.
